title: Convert List to Set: what happens to duplicates
shortTitle: What happens when you convert List to Set?
keyPoints: Converting a List to a Set removes duplicates; the Set implementation determines the resulting order
new HashSet<>(list) removes duplicates and loses order
new LinkedHashSet<>(list) removes duplicates and preserves insertion order
new TreeSet<>(list) removes duplicates and sorts the result
The first occurrence of each element is kept; later equal elements are discarded
set.size() may be less than list.size() if the list contained duplicates

s1_definition.oneliner: Converting a List to a Set removes duplicates, and the Set implementation you choose determines whether elements are unordered (HashSet), insertion-ordered (LinkedHashSet), or sorted (TreeSet).
s1_definition.profdef:
- **new HashSet<>(list)**: duplicates removed, iteration order unpredictable
- **new LinkedHashSet<>(list)**: duplicates removed, insertion order preserved
- **new TreeSet<>(list)**: duplicates removed, elements sorted by natural order or Comparator
- **stream().collect(Collectors.toSet())**: returns an unordered HashSet
- **stream().collect(Collectors.toCollection(LinkedHashSet::new))**: returns an ordered LinkedHashSet
- Duplicate detection uses equals() and hashCode() (for HashSet/LinkedHashSet) or compareTo() (for TreeSet)
s1_definition.analogy: You pour a stack of account cards – some duplicated – into a deduplicating tray. A HashSet tray keeps one of each but shuffles them. A LinkedHashSet tray keeps one of each in the order they arrived. A TreeSet tray keeps one of each sorted alphabetically.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  List → Set conversion

  List: [SAV2001, CUR3001, SAV2001, FD4001, CUR3001]
         (5 elements, 2 duplicates)
              ↓
  new HashSet<>():       {FD4001, CUR3001, SAV2001}  (no order)
  new LinkedHashSet<>(): {SAV2001, CUR3001, FD4001}  (insertion order)
  new TreeSet<>():       {CUR3001, FD4001, SAV2001}  (sorted)
              ↓
  All: 3 elements (2 duplicates removed)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Converting a List to a Set is the standard way to remove duplicates in Java. The choice of Set implementation determines the ordering: HashSet gives no ordering, LinkedHashSet preserves insertion order, and TreeSet sorts. The first occurrence of each element is kept; later equal elements are silently discarded.

In the National Bank of India's transaction reconciliation system, Rajesh receives transaction feeds from multiple channels where the same transaction may appear two or three times. He converts the list to a LinkedHashSet to get unique transactions in arrival order, then converts back to a List for the downstream processing pipeline.

The critical detail is that duplicate detection depends on equals() and hashCode(). Custom objects without proper overrides are treated as unique even when their fields are identical. Java records automatically generate correct equals and hashCode based on all components.

Remember one sentence: new LinkedHashSet<>(list) removes duplicates while keeping insertion order; the Set implementation you choose determines the ordering of the result.
